frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a 406 MHz distress beacon if it is marketed as a safety-critical emergency tool, because they prioritize safety in remote environments and are willing to pay a premium for reliable distress signaling.
T1.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, paddlers) who travel in remote areas where other communication methods are unreliable.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users already carry safety gear and are aware of the risk of isolation; a distress beacon that uses the established 406 MHz satellite network provides a credible emergency solution that can be activated with minimal effort.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the device directly to consumers at a premium price, capture recurring revenue through registration fees, and potentially license the technology to outdoor brands for co‑branding, leveraging existing distribution channels.
assumptions: Outdoor recreationists are willing to pay a premium for safety gear that reduces risk.
The 406 MHz frequency is known and trusted for emergency distress signaling.
Distribution channels (outdoor retailers, online shops) are accessible to ACR.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreationists will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point above $200.
Actual purchase rate among those who have expressed intent will be at least 10% within 12 weeks of launch.
Brand awareness of ACR among outdoor enthusiasts will increase relative to competitors.

T2.claim: Emergency responders and search-and-rescue teams will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because the frequency is standardized and provides reliable global coverage, allowing them to pinpoint isolated individuals quickly.
T2.who_benefits: Search-and-rescue agencies, emergency medical services, and law enforcement in regions where remote terrain limits other communication methods.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: These agencies already rely on satellite-based systems for distress signaling and are aware of the limitations of other frequencies; a standardized 406 MHz beacon reduces the time needed to locate a signal, potentially saving lives.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the device to government agencies and NGOs through existing procurement channels, capture recurring revenue through service contracts for beacon maintenance, and potentially license the technology to emergency equipment makers.
assumptions: 406 MHz is the internationally recognized distress frequency for satellite beacons.
Emergency responders prioritize speed of signal detection in remote areas.
Procurement cycles for emergency equipment allow for new technology adoption.
predictions: Government procurement requests for 406 MHz distress beacons will increase in the next 12 months.
Agency adoption will be driven by demonstrated search-and-rescue success stories, leading to repeat purchases.
ACR’s market share among emergency responder contracts will grow relative to competitors.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are recruited from outdoor recreation forums and mailing lists (e.g., hiking, kayaking, climbing). They are shown a description of a 406 MHz distress beacon marketed as a safety-critical emergency tool (T1) and another describing the same beacon marketed as a standardized emergency tool for search-and-rescue (T2). X1.sample: 200 participants (100 per version) recruited within 4 weeks.
X1.measure: Proportion of participants selecting option B (T1) versus option C (T2). Secondary measure: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) for each version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Proportion selecting B ≥ 55% and WTP ≥ $200; Proportion selecting C ≤ 45%.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Proportion selecting C ≥ 55% and WTP ≥ $200; Proportion selecting B ≤ 45%.

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion selecting B ≥ 55% and WTP ≥ $200, proceed with T1-focused consumer proposition. result.excerpt: (ACR) and McMurdo Limited (McMurdo) for waiver of the Commission's rules to permit the type certification of a new 406 MHz personal emergency position indicating radiobeacon (EPIRB), for the reason that the rule changes we adopt today appear to permit the equipment proposed by ACR and McMurdo.

arguments.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a 406 MHz distress beacon if it is marketed as a safety-critical emergency tool, because they prioritize safety in remote environments and are willing to pay a premium for reliable distress signaling.
arguments.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, paddlers) who travel in remote areas where other communication methods are unreliable.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: These users already carry safety gear and are aware of the risk of isolation; a distress beacon that uses the established 406 MHz satellite network provides a credible emergency solution that can be activated with minimal effort.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the device directly to consumers at a premium price, capture recurring revenue through registration fees, and potentially license the technology to outdoor brands for co‑branding, leveraging existing distribution channels.
assumptions: Outdoor recreationists are willing to pay a premium for safety gear that reduces risk.
The 406 MHz frequency is known and trusted for emergency distress signaling.
Distribution channels (outdoor retailers, online shops) are accessible to ACR.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreationists will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point above $200.
Actual purchase rate among those who have expressed intent will be at least 10% within 12 weeks of launch.
Brand awareness of ACR among outdoor enthusiasts will increase relative to competitors.

arguments.claim: Emergency responders and search-and-rescue teams will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because the frequency is standardized and provides reliable global coverage, allowing them to pinpoint isolated individuals quickly.
arguments.who_benefits: Search-and-rescue agencies, emergency medical services, and law enforcement in regions where remote terrain limits other communication methods.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: These agencies already rely on satellite-based systems for distress signaling and are aware of the limitations of other frequencies; a standardized 406 MHz beacon reduces the time needed to locate a signal, potentially saving lives.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the device to government agencies and NGOs through existing procurement channels, capture recurring revenue through service contracts for beacon maintenance, and potentially license the technology to emergency equipment makers.
assumptions: 406 MHz is the internationally recognized distress frequency for satellite beacons.
Emergency responders prioritize speed of signal detection in remote areas.
Procurement cycles for emergency equipment allow for new technology adoption.
predictions: Government procurement requests for 406 MHz distress beacons will increase in the next 12 months.
Agency adoption will be driven by demonstrated search-and-rescue success stories, leading to repeat purchases.
ACR’s market share among emergency responder contracts will grow relative to competitors.

arguments.quote: The 406 MHz PLB is primarily intended to provide a distress and alerting capacity for use by the general public in life threatening situations in a remote environment after all other means of notifying SAR responders (e.g., telephone, radio) have been exhausted.
arguments.does_not_show: It does not show that outdoor recreationists specifically would adopt the device, nor that they would pay a premium price.

arguments.sample: 200 participants (100 per version) recruited within 4 weeks.
arguments.measure: Proportion of participants selecting option B (T1) versus option C (T2). Secondary measure: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) for each version.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer and willingness-to-pay questions, followed by a limited pilot distribution of beacons to outdoor recreationists and emergency responder contacts.
X1.sample: 500 outdoor recreationists (recruited via outdoor forums and clubs) and 200 emergency responder contacts (recruited via SAR agencies and distributors).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreationists would show ≥20% pre-order rate and willingness to pay premium.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Emergency responders would show ≥15% order rate and willingness to pay premium.

X1.decision_rule: If outdoor recreation pre-order rate ≥20% AND emergency responder order rate ≥15%, proceed with differentiated consumer product development. If either rate falls below 15%, focus on B2B/B2G expansion or no expansion.

final.target_customer: Outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, sailors) and emergency responders (coast guard, search-and-rescue teams)
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon that combines reliable emergency signaling with safety-enhancing features (e.g., GPS, strobe light) and complies with regulatory standards, sold at a premium price through outdoor retailers and distributors.
final.next_action: Run the 12‑week pilot test (X1) with 500 outdoor recreationists and 200 emergency responder contacts, measuring pre-order rates and willingness to pay.
final.uncertainty: Both demand segments are uncertain due to lack of direct evidence; the pilot will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the pilot shows <15% pre-order rate for outdoor recreationists or <15% order rate for emergency responders, the recommendation would shift to focus on B2B/B2G expansion or no expansion.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.

Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Outdoor Recreation vs. Commercial Marine
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Outdoor Recreation Group (recruited from outdoor enthusiast forums and outdoor retailer mailing lists) and Commercial Marine Group (recruited from marine industry newsletters and safety equipment distributors). Each participant views a product description of a 406 MHz PLB (specifying its distress capability, FCC approval, and price point of €300) and is asked: "Would you purchase this device for personal use?" (Yes/No).
X1.sample: 200 participants (100 per group). Outdoor Recreation Group: 100 registered outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, paddlers, climbers) who have participated in activities where emergency response is limited. Commercial Marine Group: 100 professionals (marine operators, crew members, search and rescue personnel) who work in environments where reliable distress signaling is required.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (Yes) and willingness to pay (WTP) measured as a percentage of participants who would buy the device at the given price point.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor Recreation Group will show a purchase intent rate ≥50% and a WTP ≥50% at €300; Commercial Marine Group will show a purchase intent rate <30% and a WTP <50% at €300.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Commercial Marine Group will show a purchase intent rate ≥40% and a WTP ≥50% at €300; Outdoor Recreation Group will show a purchase intent rate <30% and a WTP <50% at €300.

X1.decision_rule: If Outdoor Recreation Group purchase intent ≥50% AND WTP ≥50% at €300, proceed with consumer proposition for outdoor recreation. If Commercial Marine Group purchase intent ≥40% AND WTP ≥50% at €300, proceed with compliance-grade consumer proposition for marine operators. If neither group meets both thresholds, recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, price sensitivity, or adoption behavior for outdoor recreation users. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed consumer preference survey (Test X1) to validate demand before committing resources. If the survey meets the thresholds, proceed with a limited launch of a consumer-branded distress beacon; otherwise, maintain the existing B2B/B2G focus.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation participants (hikers, paddlers, climbers) who engage in activities where emergency response is limited and are willing to pay a premium for reliable distress signaling.
final.value_proposition: A premium-priced, easy-to-use 406 MHz distress beacon that leverages ACR’s existing PLB technology to provide reliable distress signaling in remote environments, sold through outdoor retailers and online channels.
final.next_action: Run the consumer preference survey (Test X1) within the 12‑week budget of €15,000 to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a €300 device.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and price sensitivity. The survey will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the survey shows <30% purchase intent or <50% willingness to pay at €300 for the outdoor group, we would abandon T1 and focus on the marine/commercial segment (supporting T2).
If the survey shows ≥50% purchase intent and ≥50% willingness to pay for the outdoor group, we would proceed with a consumer launch based on T1.
If new evidence emerges showing strong demand from marine operators or personal safety professionals, we would reconsider T2.

arguments.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Outdoor recreation group receiving a product description emphasizing safety-critical, regulatory compliance, and outdoor use; (B) SAR group receiving a product description emphasizing standardized distress signal integration for search-and-rescue teams. Both descriptions include price point (e.g., €350) and a
X1.sample: 200 respondents: 100 self-identified outdoor recreation enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor activity forums) and 100 emergency responders/search-and-rescue personnel (recruited via professional associations).
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1‑“Very unlikely” to 7‑“Very likely”). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than SAR group.
prediction_by_theory.T2: SAR group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than outdoor group.

X1.decision_rule: If outdoor group’s average purchase intent ≥ 5.5 and WTP ≥ €300, proceed to develop a consumer-focused outdoor distress beacon. If SAR group’s average purchase intent ≥ 5.5 and WTP ≥ €300, proceed to develop a SAR‑integrated distress beacon. If neither group meets both thresholds, recommend no expansion.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed consumer preference survey (Test X1) to validate demand before committing resources. final.value_proposition: A portable, safety-certified 406 MHz distress beacon marketed as a critical tool for remote travel, emphasizing regulatory compliance, emergency reliability, and integration with outdoor gear.
final.next_action: Run the consumer preference survey (Test X1) within the 12‑week timeframe and €15,000 budget, using the decision rule to determine whether to proceed with a consumer product or maintain the existing portfolio.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence of consumer demand or SAR adoption in 2002. The survey results will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the survey shows outdoor group purchase intent <5.5 or WTP <€300, the recommendation would shift to no expansion.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Outdoor Recreation vs SAR Distress Beacon
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Outdoor recreation group receiving a product description emphasizing safety-critical, regulatory compliance, and outdoor use; (B) SAR group receiving a product description emphasizing standardized distress signal integration for search-and-rescue teams. Both descriptions include price point (e.g., €350) and a
arguments.sample: 200 respondents: 100 self-identified outdoor recreation enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor activity forums) and 100 emergency responders/search-and-rescue personnel (recruited via professional associations).
arguments.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1‑“Very unlikely” to 7‑“Very likely”). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than SAR group.
prediction_by_theory.T2: SAR group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than outdoor group.

arguments.decision_rule: If outdoor group’s average purchase intent ≥ 5.5 and WTP ≥ €300, proceed to develop a consumer-focused outdoor distress beacon. If SAR group’s average purchase intent ≥ 5.5 and WTP ≥ €300, proceed to develop a SAR‑integrated distress beacon. If neither group meets both thresholds, recommend no expansion.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed consumer preference survey (Test X1) to validate demand before committing resources. If the survey meets the thresholds (outdoor group purchase intent ≥5.5, WTP ≥€300), proceed to develop a consumer-focused outdoor distress beacon; otherwise, maintain current portfolio and focus on B2B/B2G segments.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify current reach to individual buyers from public sources.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home gardening, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales or new dealer partnerships).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current B2B dealer model and existing product lines.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., automotive or recreational vehicle manufacturers).

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they perceive them as a practical, inexpensive tool for multiple tasks, and they can purchase them through existing dealer networks without requiring new channels.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners gain a versatile, low‑cost device for yard work; Deere benefits by selling through its existing dealer network, avoiding new distribution costs.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rapidly increasing small‑garden households need a tool that can handle various chores; the tractor's low price and ease of use make it attractive compared to manual tools.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere captures value by selling tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging existing relationships and avoiding the need for new retail channels.
assumptions: Small‑garden households in 1962 have sufficient disposable income to afford a lawn tractor.
Deere's dealer network is willing and able to stock and sell lawn tractors.
Consumers trust Deere's brand for agricultural equipment and will extend that trust to lawn and garden products.
predictions: If Deere introduces a lawn and garden tractor, dealers will order sufficient units to meet demand within 12 weeks.

T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere captures value by selling tractors through its existing dealer network, positioning the product as a consumer convenience rather than a farm tool, and earning premium pricing for a differentiated offering.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify current reach to individual buyers from public sources.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home gardening, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales or new dealer partnerships).

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rapidly increasing demand for garden tractors indicates that homeowners are willing to purchase a product that solves multiple gardening tasks.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can sell directly to consumers through existing dealers, offering a lower-margin consumer product that broadens its customer base and diversifies revenue.
assumptions: Homeowners in 1962 have disposable income to purchase a small tractor.
Maintenance costs of early garden tractors are acceptable compared to manual tools.
Deere can source or design a simple, affordable tractor without disrupting its core farm equipment business.
predictions: If Deere launches a consumer-focused garden tractor, sales will exceed 1,000 units within 12 months in the United States.
Surveyed homeowners will rank the tractor as "most useful" for tasks like clearing weeds, mowing small areas, and moving soil.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractor
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a basic lawn and garden tractor (price $500, features: small engine, manual controls, no attachments). They are asked: "Which benefit matters most to you when considering a lawn and garden tractor?" (A) Cost-effectiveness and practicality for small gardens; (B) Status symbol and modern home improvement; (C) None of the above. They also rate the tractor on a 1‑10‑
X1.sample: 200 U.S. homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region. Participants must have a small garden (under 1,000 sq ft) and disposable income to purchase a $500 item.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: the proportion of participants who select (A) Cost-effectiveness and practicality as their top benefit. Secondary outcomes: average rating of status/modernity (1‑10) and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 60% of participants will select (A) as their top benefit, and the average WTP will be below $600.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 40% of participants will select (B) as their top benefit, and the average WTP will be above $700.

X1.decision_rule: If the observed proportion selecting (A) is ≥ 60% and the average WTP ≤ $600, proceed with a consumer‑focused, cost‑effective garden tractor proposition. If the observed proportion selecting (B) is ≥ 40% and the average WTP ≥ $700, proceed with a premium‑priced, status‑oriented

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed consumer preference survey (Test X1) to validate demand for a cost-effective garden tractor before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Small-garden homeowners (under 1,000 sq ft) with disposable income to purchase a $500 item.
final.value_proposition: A basic lawn and garden tractor priced at $500 that is easy to use for small gardens, offering cost-effectiveness and practicality.
final.next_action: Run the consumer preference survey (Test X1) within 12 weeks, targeting 200 U.S. homeowners with small gardens and disposable income.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence from 1962 about homeowner motivations. The survey will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the survey shows at least 60% selecting cost-effectiveness and practicality as their top benefit, and average willingness to pay below $600, proceed with a consumer-focused, cost-effective garden tractor proposition.
If the survey shows at least 40% selecting status/modernity as their top benefit and average willingness to pay above $700, consider a premium-priced, status-oriented offering.

X1.method: Online survey of 200 small‑garden homeowners (households with under 1‑acre yards) in the Midwest. Participants are recruited via a panel to match 1962 demographics. They are shown a description of a lawn and garden tractor (specifications, price, and a photo) and asked: "Would you purchase this tractor through your current John Deere dealer?" (Yes/No). They also rate perceived convenience (1‑5) and willingness to pay (1‑5).
X1.sample: 200 homeowners, balanced for age, gender, and household income (approx. $20,000–$40,000).
X1.measure: Purchase intent (Yes/No) and willingness to pay (WTP) in dollars.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 40% of participants will indicate purchase intent through the dealer, and the average WTP will be above $1,500 (reflecting 1962 price points).
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 40% of participants will indicate purchase intent through the dealer, and the average WTP will be above $1,500, with a higher proportion (e.g., >50%) citing convenience as the primary reason.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent ≥ 40% and average WTP ≥ $1,500, both theories are supported. If only purchase intent meets the threshold, T1 is more likely. If only WTP meets the threshold, T2 is more likely. If neither meets the threshold, both theories are rejected.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, dealer networks, or purchase intent for lawn and garden tractors. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Conduct the proposed Dealer Survey Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay among small‑garden homeowners. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify current reach to individual buyers from public sources.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home gardening, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales or new dealer partnerships).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current B2B dealer model and existing product lines.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., automotive or recreational vehicle manufacturers).

T1.claim: Homeowners with small gardens will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for multiple chores, and easy to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking affordable, versatile garden tools; Deere benefits by selling tractors directly or through dealers, capturing higher margins than bulk farm equipment.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rapidly rising sales of garden tractors (76% growth 1960-1979) indicates homeowners shift from manual tools to powered equipment; the low cost and multi-use capability make the shift attractive.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can price tractors modestly and sell accessories, earning revenue from a new consumer segment while leveraging existing tractor engineering.
assumptions: Small-garden homeowners have sufficient disposable income to purchase a tractor.
They value time-saving and multi-use functionality.
Deere can reach this segment through existing dealer network or new direct channels.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to pay a price point comparable to early 1960s consumer goods for a garden tractor.
Pilot sales of a basic garden tractor will exceed dealer expectations within 12 weeks.
Accessory sales (e.g., mower blades, snow blowers) will be higher than for farm tractors.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Convenience is a primary driver of consumer adoption; if a tool reduces time spent on tasks, consumers are willing to adopt it even at higher cost.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify current reach to individual buyers from public sources.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home gardening, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales or new dealer partnerships).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current B2B dealer model and existing product lines.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., automotive or recreational vehicle manufacturers).

T1.claim: Small‑scale farmers will purchase tractors directly from Deere because they need specialized equipment for specific tasks and trust Deere’s engineering.
T1.who_benefits: Deere benefits by selling tractors directly to farmers at premium prices, bypassing dealers and capturing higher margins.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Farmers gain access to Deere’s proven tractor technology and service support, reducing reliance on dealers and perceived savings.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells tractors at higher retail prices and retains control over the sales channel, limiting dealer markup and potential price erosion.
assumptions: Small‑scale farmers have sufficient capital to purchase a tractor directly.
Deere can service and support tractors sold directly without major infrastructure changes.
Trust in Deere’s brand and engineering outweighs dealer presence for this segment.
predictions: If Deere launches a direct‑to‑farmer offering, purchase rates among small‑scale farmers will increase compared to existing dealer model.
Deere will achieve higher average transaction value per tractor sold directly.

T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells tractors at retail prices, captures brand premium, and controls the sales channel, limiting dealer discounts and potential price erosion.
assumptions: Homeowners have sufficient disposable income for a tractor purchase.
Deere can market and service tractors directly to homeowners without major changes.
Brand trust outweighs dealer presence for this segment.
predictions: If Deere launches a direct‑to‑consumer offering, purchase rates among homeowners will increase compared to the existing dealer model.
